front: Define **factors of production**.
back: The **factors of production** are the resources used by businesses to produce goods and services.

front: Define **capital**.
back: **Capital** includes any man-made resource used to produce goods and services, such as tools, buildings, machines and computer equipment.

front: Define **land**.
back: **Land** includes the natural resources and physical locations that are used for production.

front: Define **labour**.
back: **Labour** is the human input into the production process, involving mental or physical effort.

front: Define **enterprise**.
back: **Enterprise** involves taking risks when setting up or running a business, with the entrepreneur combining the factors of production to generate profit.

front: How many factors of production are there?
back: There are **four** factors of production: capital, enterprise, land and labour.

front: What determines the effectiveness of labour?
back: The effectiveness of labour is determined by the **education, training and experience** that workers have.

front: What is the factor income earned by land?
back: The factor income earned by land is **rent**.

front: What is the reward for enterprise?
back: The reward for enterprise is **profit**.

front:
**True or False?**

The reward for capital is interest.
back:
**True.**

The factor income earned by capital is interest.

front:
**True or False?**

Producing a good or service usually requires only one factor of production.
back:
**False.**

The production of any good or service requires a combination of all four factors of production.

front: The factor income earned by labour is <u>  </u>.
back: The factor income earned by labour is **wages**.

front: Define the **primary sector**.
back: The **primary sector** is concerned with the extraction of raw materials from land, sea or air, such as farming, mining or fishing.

front: Define the **secondary sector**.
back: The **secondary sector** is concerned with the processing of raw materials and the manufacture of goods, such as oil refinement and vehicle production.

front: Define the **tertiary sector**.
back: The **tertiary sector** is concerned with the provision of services for consumers and other businesses, such as leisure, banking or hospitality.

front: Define the **chain of production**.
back: The **chain of production** is the series of steps taken to turn raw materials into a finished product that can be marketed and sold.

front: In which sector would a coal miner work?
back: A coal miner would work in the **primary sector**, as mining involves the extraction of raw materials.

front: Which sector links the primary and tertiary sectors in the chain of production?
back: The **secondary sector** links them, as it processes and manufactures the raw materials extracted by the primary sector.

front: On which sector is a less developed economy primarily focused?
back: A less developed economy is primarily focused on the **primary sector**, with most people employed in agriculture.

front: Why do successive sectors tend to generate higher profits?
back: Successive sectors tend to generate higher profits because each sector **adds more value** than the previous one.

front: Why do many firms relocate manufacturing to emerging economies?
back: Many firms relocate manufacturing to emerging economies to take advantage of the **lower average wage rates** there.

front:
**True or False?**

The most developed economies have a very high proportion of the workforce employed in services.
back:
**True.**

Developed economies fund advanced education and higher-level skills training, which supports the growth of service industries.

front:
**True or False?**

As economies develop, employment shifts from the tertiary sector towards the primary sector.
back:
**False.**

As economies develop, employment shifts away from the primary sector towards the secondary and then the tertiary sector.

front: In emerging economies, improved technology means that less <u>  </u> is required in the primary sector.
back: In emerging economies, improved technology means that less **labour** is required in the primary sector, so more workers move into manufacturing.

front: The movement of firms from one sector of the economy to another is known as <u>  </u>.
back: The movement of firms from one sector of the economy to another is known as **sectoral change**.

front: Define **production**.
back: **Production** refers to the volume of output produced using the factors of production.

front: Define **productivity**.
back: **Productivity** is the output per unit of input of a resource in a given time period, i.e. the rate at which output is produced.

front: Define **investment in human capital**.
back: **Investment in human capital** occurs when firms spend money on training their labour to improve efficiency and skill levels.

front: What is productivity used to measure?
back: Productivity is used to measure the **efficiency of production methods**.

front: Name two common measures of productivity.
back: Two common measures of productivity are **labour productivity** and **capital productivity**.

front: How can the productivity of land be improved?
back: The productivity of land can be improved by raising its quality, for example through greater use of **fertiliser, drainage or irrigation**.

front: How does process innovation affect productivity?
back: Process innovation often results in **productivity improvements**, such as moving from labour-intensive to automated car production.

front: How does an increase in productivity affect the production possibilities curve?
back: An increase in productivity causes an **outward shift** of the production possibilities curve, as more can be produced with existing factors.

front:
**True or False?**

Production and productivity mean the same thing.
back:
**False.**

Production is the total volume of output, whereas productivity is the output per unit of input in a given time period.

front:
**True or False?**

Investment in the training of workers is likely to increase labour productivity.
back:
**True.**

Training improves the quality of labour, increasing the speed at which output is produced.

front: A positive net migration rate of <u>  </u> labour will increase the quality of labour available.
back: A positive net migration rate of **skilled** labour will increase the quality of labour available.

front: A fall in the quantity or quality of factors of production causes an <u>  </u> shift of the production possibilities curve.
back: A fall in the quantity or quality of factors of production causes an **inward** shift of the production possibilities curve.

front: Define the **division of labour**.
back: The **division of labour** occurs when a task is broken up into several component tasks.

front: Define **specialisation**.
back: **Specialisation** occurs when workers focus on one or a few components of the production process and thereby gain significant skill in doing it.

front: Which economist developed the ideas of specialisation and the division of labour?
back: **Adam Smith** developed the ideas of specialisation and the division of labour, based on observations at a pin factory.

front: How does the division of labour affect productivity?
back: The division of labour raises output per worker, and so **increases productivity**.

front: At what levels can specialisation occur?
back: Specialisation can occur at the **individual, business, regional and global** levels.

front: How does the division of labour lower a firm's cost per unit?
back: Higher labour productivity from the division of labour **lowers the cost per unit**, making the firm's goods more price competitive.

front: Give one benefit of the division of labour for workers.
back: Workers can **acquire the single skill required relatively quickly** and gain recognition and status for performing it well.

front: How can the division of labour lead to structural unemployment?
back: If entire industries close because firms cannot compete with cheaper labour abroad, workers with a limited skill base face **structural unemployment**.

front:
**True or False?**

The division of labour can make work repetitive and boring for workers.
back:
**True.**

Repetitive work can lower motivation and productivity, and may lead to high staff turnover.

front:
**True or False?**

The division of labour increases the time firms must spend training new workers.
back:
**False.**

The division of labour reduces training time, because each worker only needs to learn a single, narrow task.

front: For firms, the increased output from the division of labour helps generate more sales and <u>  </u>.
back: For firms, the increased output from the division of labour helps generate more sales and **profit**.

front: If a firm replaces labour with <u>  </u>, a worker with a limited skill base may struggle to find employment elsewhere.
back: If a firm replaces labour with **capital**, a worker with a limited skill base may struggle to find employment elsewhere.

front: Bangladesh specialises in <u>  </u> and exports them globally.
back: Bangladesh specialises in **textiles** and exports them globally.

front: Define **fixed costs**.
back: **Fixed costs** are costs that do not change as the level of output changes, such as rent, insurance and management salaries.

front: Define **variable costs**.
back: **Variable costs** are costs that vary directly with output, such as raw materials and the wages of workers directly involved in production.

front: Define **total cost**.
back: **Total cost** is the sum of total fixed costs and total variable costs.

front: Define **total revenue**.
back: **Total revenue** is the total value of all sales a firm generates, calculated as selling price multiplied by quantity sold.

front: Define **average revenue**.
back: **Average revenue** is the overall revenue per unit, and is the technical economic name for **price**.

front: What is the formula for average total cost?
back: The formula for **average total cost** is **total cost divided by quantity (TC ÷ Q)**.

front: What is the formula for total variable cost?
back: **Total variable cost** is calculated as **variable cost per unit multiplied by quantity (VC × Q)**.

front: When does a firm break even?
back: A firm **breaks even** when **total revenue equals total costs (TR = TC)**, covering all its costs without making a profit or a loss.

front: How is profit calculated?
back: **Profit** is calculated as **total revenue minus total costs (TR − TC)**.

front:
**True or False?**

Total costs can never be zero because all firms have some fixed costs.
back:
**True.**

Even at zero output a firm must still pay its fixed costs, so total costs can never fall to zero.

front:
**True or False?**

Fixed costs increase as output increases.
back:
**False.**

Fixed costs stay the same regardless of output; it is variable costs that increase as output increases.

front: Average revenue is the technical economic name for <u>  </u>.
back: Average revenue is the technical economic name for **price**.

front: Average revenue is especially useful to a firm selling <u>  </u> products, such as a supermarket.
back: Average revenue is especially useful to a firm selling **multiple** products, such as a supermarket.

front: Define **economies of scale**.
back: **Economies of scale** are the efficiencies a firm gains as it increases its scale of output, which lower its average cost of production.

front: Define **diseconomies of scale**.
back: **Diseconomies of scale** occur when a firm increases its scale of output beyond a certain point, causing its average costs to rise.

front: Define **internal economies of scale**.
back: **Internal economies of scale** occur as a result of the growth in the scale of production within the firm itself.

front: Define **external economies of scale**.
back: **External economies of scale** arise from external changes in the locality and industry that lower a firm's average costs as the industry grows.

front: Define **internal diseconomies of scale**.
back: **Internal diseconomies of scale** occur when an increase in the scale of output raises the cost per unit due to factors generated inside the business.

front: How does a purchasing economy of scale lower average cost?
back: A **purchasing economy of scale** lowers average cost because large firms buy raw materials in greater volumes and receive a **bulk purchase discount**.

front: Why do large firms enjoy a financial economy of scale?
back: Large firms enjoy a **financial economy of scale** because they often receive **lower interest rates** on loans, as they are perceived as less risky.

front: Give one source of external economies of scale.
back: One source of **external economies of scale** is a local supply of **skilled labour**, as local educational establishments train workers for the industry.

front: How does bureaucracy create a diseconomy of scale?
back: **Bureaucracy** creates a diseconomy of scale because significant paperwork, rules and regulations slow down decision making and production, raising average cost.

front:
**True or False?**

Economies of scale cause a firm's average costs to rise.
back:
**False.**

Economies of scale lower a firm's average cost of production; it is diseconomies of scale that raise average costs.

front:
**True or False?**

External economies of scale result from the growth of the whole industry rather than the individual firm.
back:
**True.**

External economies of scale come from changes in the locality and industry, whereas internal economies of scale come from the growth of the firm itself.

front: Managerial economies of scale occur when large firms employ <u>  </u> managers who are more efficient at certain tasks.
back: Managerial economies of scale occur when large firms employ **specialist** managers who are more efficient at certain tasks.

front: Internal diseconomies of scale cause the average cost per unit to <u>  </u>.
back: Internal diseconomies of scale cause the average cost per unit to **rise**.

front: Define **competition**.
back: **Competition** refers to the number of firms that sell **similar products** in the same industry.

front: Define a **competitive market**.
back: A **competitive market** is one with many firms selling similar products, forcing them to work hard to **keep and attract customers**.

front: Give one disadvantage of competitive markets for consumers.
back: One disadvantage is **too much choice**, which can overwhelm consumers so they stick to products they already know.

front: Why does competition tend to lower prices for consumers?
back: Competition tends to lower prices because firms **cut prices in an attempt to gain market share**.

front: Give two advantages of competitive markets for firms.
back: Two advantages of competitive markets for firms are **greater efficiency** (lower costs of production) and **increased innovation** to attract new customers.

front: How can competition improve the standard of living in an economy?
back: Competition improves the standard of living because **innovation and improved goods and services** become available in markets over time.

front: Give one disadvantage of competitive markets for workers.
back: A disadvantage for workers is that **low profit margins may result in low wages and poor working environments**.

front:
**True or False?**

Too much competition can reduce profit levels and stifle innovation.
back:
**True.**

Very low profit margins caused by excessive competition can stifle innovation and economic progress.

front:
**True or False?**

Competition always guarantees higher product quality for consumers.
back:
**False.**

In a bid to lower prices, product quality may deteriorate as firms cut costs or use cheaper raw materials.

front: For consumers, more sellers in a competitive market means more <u>  </u>.
back: For consumers, more sellers in a competitive market means more **choice**.

front: To keep their costs low in a competitive market, firms are likely to minimise <u>  </u>.
back: To keep their costs low in a competitive market, firms are likely to minimise **waste**.

front: In a crowded market, firms continuously seek to improve the <u>  </u> of their goods to become recognised.
back: In a crowded market, firms continuously seek to improve the **quality** of their goods to become recognised.

front: Define **market capitalisation**.
back: **Market capitalisation** is the market value of a company, calculated by **multiplying the number of shares issued by the share price**.

front: Define **market share**.
back: **Market share** is the **percentage of total sales** in an industry that is held by a particular firm.

front: Define a **merger**.
back: A **merger** is when two firms **combine into a single business entity**, which creates rapid growth.

front: Name three metrics used to measure the size of a firm.
back: Three metrics used to measure firm size are the **number of employees**, **market share**, and the **size of profits** (or market capitalisation).

front: How many employees does a firm generally have to be classed as large?
back: A firm is generally classed as **large** when it has **more than 500 employees**.

front: Give one advantage a small firm has over a large firm.
back: A small firm can offer **highly customised goods and services** and build **personal relationships** with customers, generating loyalty.

front: Why might a large firm be able to charge lower prices than a small firm?
back: A large firm can benefit from **economies of scale** that lower its cost per unit, and it may pass these savings on as **lower prices**.

front: How does growth allow a firm to spread risk?
back: Growth allows **product diversification**, so if one product fails **others may still be successful**, reducing risk.

front: Give one reason an entrepreneur might choose to keep their firm small.
back: An owner may keep a firm small because their aim is **an acceptable quality of life or satisficing** rather than profit maximisation.

front:
**True or False?**

A firm that grows too large may experience diseconomies of scale.
back:
**True.**

When a firm grows too large it may face difficulties coordinating departments and controlling quality, raising average costs.

front:
**True or False?**

Small firms find it easier to access large bank loans than large firms.
back:
**False.**

Small firms have fewer financial resources and less access to large loans; some cannot access any loans at all.

front: Larger firms can take advantage of economies of scale to lower their average <u>  </u>.
back: Larger firms can take advantage of economies of scale to lower their average **costs**.

front: Firms may take over or merge with rivals because they desire stronger market <u>  </u> and fewer competitors.
back: Firms may take over or merge with rivals because they desire stronger market **power** and fewer competitors.

front: Governments monitor merger activity to prevent a single firm gaining a significant market <u>  </u>.
back: Governments monitor merger activity to prevent a single firm gaining a significant market **share**.

front: Define **monopoly**.
back: A **monopoly** is a market structure in which a **single seller dominates the market**.

front: Define **price-maker**.
back: A **price-maker** is a firm with complete market power that can **set the price of its product** rather than accept the market price.

front: Define **barriers to entry**.
back: **Barriers to entry** are obstacles, such as patents or high start-up costs, that **prevent or deter competitors** from entering a market.

front: What percentage of market share do many governments use to define a monopoly?
back: Many governments define a monopoly as any firm having **more than 25% market share**.

front: How can a monopoly's large profits benefit the products consumers receive?
back: A monopoly's large profits can be invested in **research and development**. This may lead to **product innovation and better quality products** for consumers.

front: Why are a monopoly's high profits not eroded in the long run?
back: A monopoly's high profits are not eroded because **high barriers to entry prevent competitors from entering** the industry.

front: Give one advantage of a monopoly for consumers.
back: A monopoly can achieve **economies of scale**, which lowers average cost and may lead to **lower prices** if savings are passed on.

front: Why might a monopoly lead to higher prices?
back: A monopoly may lead to higher prices because a **lack of competition and no substitute goods** allow the firm to raise prices.

front:
**True or False?**

A monopolist sells a product that has close substitutes.
back:
**False.**

A monopoly sells a unique product for which there are no substitute products.

front:
**True or False?**

A lack of competition can reduce a monopoly's incentive to be cost efficient.
back:
**True.**

With no competitive pressure, a monopoly has a reduced incentive to control costs and improve efficiency.

front: In a monopoly, a single seller has complete market <u>  </u>.
back: In a monopoly, a single seller has complete market **power**.

front: A monopoly may limit supply in order to increase <u>  </u>, leading to an inefficient allocation of resources.
back: A monopoly may limit supply in order to increase **price**, leading to an inefficient allocation of resources.

front: A monopoly may offer worse customer <u>  </u> because the incentive to improve it is limited.
back: A monopoly may offer worse customer **service** because the incentive to improve it is limited.

front: Define **oligopoly**.
back: An **oligopoly** is a market structure where a **small number of large firms dominate** the industry.

front: Define **concentration ratio**.
back: A **concentration ratio** calculates the **percentage of total market share** served by a specific number of the largest firms.

front: Define **interdependence** in an oligopoly.
back: **Interdependence** means that oligopolists **study and respond to each other's behaviour** when making decisions.

front: Define a **price war**.
back: A **price war** occurs when competitors repeatedly **lower prices to undercut each other**, resulting in all firms achieving lower profits.

front: Define **predatory pricing**.
back: **Predatory pricing** is when a firm temporarily reduces its price, often below cost, to **drive out an existing competitor**, and is illegal.

front: Give an example of an industry in the UK that is an oligopoly.
back: The UK **supermarket industry** is an oligopoly, dominated by firms such as Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda and Morrisons.

front: Why are exit barriers high in an oligopoly?
back: Exit barriers are high because of large **sunk costs** that firms cannot recoup if they leave the industry.

front: What is the most common form of competition used by oligopolists?
back: The most common form of competition used by oligopolists is **non-price competition**, focused on product differentiation.

front: How does limit pricing differ from predatory pricing?
back: **Limit pricing** temporarily lowers prices to **prevent a new competitor from entering**, whereas predatory pricing aims to drive out an existing rival.

front: Give one advantage of an oligopoly for consumers.
back: Consumers may benefit from **lower prices**, as large-scale operations create economies of scale that reduce average costs.

front:
**True or False?**

Oligopolists have a strong incentive to collude in order to increase profits.
back:
**True.**

With few competitors, oligopolists have a strong incentive to collude, as this can lead to greater profits.

front:
**True or False?**

Products in an oligopoly are usually undifferentiated and identical.
back:
**False.**

Products tend to be highly differentiated through branding, so consumers perceive them as different and become brand loyal.

front: Non-price competition in an oligopoly focuses on product <u>  </u> to build brand loyalty.
back: Non-price competition in an oligopoly focuses on product **differentiation** to build brand loyalty.

front: High barriers to entry in an oligopoly can restrict the number of firms and result in low <u>  </u>.
back: High barriers to entry in an oligopoly can restrict the number of firms and result in low **innovation**.

front: Define **quality of labour**.
back: The **quality of labour** refers to the **skills, knowledge and expertise** of workers.

front: Define **quantity of labour**.
back: The **quantity of labour** refers to the **number of available workers** to a business.

front: Define **education**.
back: **Education** occurs in **schools and universities** and may be funded by the government or run by private educational firms.

front: Define **training**.
back: **Training** is undertaken by firms and shapes the **skills and knowledge** of human capital and the **quality of labour**.

front: Why are labour costs important to a firm?
back: Labour costs are important because they often represent one of the **most significant business costs**.

front: How can a firm lower its labour costs?
back: A firm can lower its labour costs by **increasing the productivity of workers** or by **reducing wages and salaries**.

front: What is the effect of a higher quality of labour on a business?
back: A higher quality of labour raises the **potential productivity** of the business.

front: How can more skilled workers benefit a business?
back: More skilled workers can **drive innovation**, creating a **competitive advantage** for businesses.

front:
**True or False?**

Multinational firms may locate near top universities to access highly skilled workers.
back:
**True.**

Tech multinationals such as Google and Microsoft have located near Paris universities to access **highly skilled** workers. This raises the quality of labour available to them.

front:
**True or False?**

The quantity of labour refers to the skills and expertise of workers.
back:
**False.**

The quantity of labour refers to the **number of available workers**; skills and expertise describe the **quality** of labour.

front:
**True or False?**

Where university education is free, firms benefit from reduced training costs for some specialist workers.
back:
**True.**

In countries like Sweden and Denmark, **free university education** means firms face **reduced training costs** for some specialist workers.

front: Multinational companies may set up production in countries like Bangladesh or Vietnam due to the large <u>  </u> availability at low wages.
back: Multinational companies may set up production in countries like Bangladesh or Vietnam due to the large **labour force** availability at low wages.

front: Some countries invest less in education, which puts the <u>  </u> to spend more on education and training.
back: Some countries invest less in education, which puts the **burden on business** to spend more on education and training.

front: Define **derived demand**.
back: **Derived demand** means the demand for labour **depends on the demand for the goods and services** it helps produce.

front: Define the **labour market**.
back: The **labour market** is composed of **sellers of labour** (households) and **buyers of labour** (firms).

front: Give an example of the demand for labour being a derived demand.
back: As the demand for technology devices rises, technology firms **demand more skilled labour** to design, manufacture and market the products.

front: What happens to the demand for labour if demand for goods and services increases?
back: If demand for goods and services increases, the **demand for labour will also increase**, because labour demand is derived.

front: What is the relationship between the wage rate and the quantity of labour demanded?
back: There is an **inverse relationship**: as the wage rate rises, the **quantity of labour demanded falls**.

front: What causes a movement along the demand curve for labour?
back: A **change in the wage rate** alone causes a **movement along** the demand curve for labour.

front: How does an increase in the selling price of a product affect the demand for labour?
back: A higher selling price incentivises the firm to supply more, so the **demand for labour increases** and the curve **shifts right**.

front: How does substituting capital for labour affect labour demand?
back: If capital (machinery) is more cost effective, the **demand for labour decreases** and the demand curve **shifts left**.

front:
**True or False?**

A shift of the labour demand curve to the right means more workers are employed at each wage rate.
back:
**True.**

A rightward shift means **more workers** are employed at each wage rate.

front:
**True or False?**

A change in the wage rate alone shifts the entire demand curve for labour.
back:
**False.**

A change in the wage rate alone causes a **movement along** the curve; other factors shift the whole curve.

front:
**True or False?**

Clothing manufacturers in Bangladesh and Vietnam have invested in automated production to reduce their demand for labour.
back:
**True.**

By substituting capital for labour, these firms **reduce their demand for labour** and save on labour costs. The labour demand curve shifts left.

front: An increase in online shopping caused a rightward <u>  </u> in the demand for labour to deliver goods.
back: An increase in online shopping caused a rightward **shift** in the demand for labour to deliver goods.

front: When an economy is in a <u>  </u>, demand for most goods and services falls and the demand for labour decreases.
back: When an economy is in a **recession**, demand for most goods and services falls and the demand for labour decreases.

front: Define the **supply curve for labour**.
back: The **supply curve for labour** shows the relationship between the **wage rate** and the **number of workers** willing to work in an occupation.

front: Define **geographical mobility of labour**.
back: **Geographical mobility of labour** is the ease with which workers can **move from one geographical area to another** to secure employment.

front: Define **occupational mobility of labour**.
back: **Occupational mobility of labour** is the ability of a worker to **change occupations** when they lose a job.

front: What is the relationship between the wage rate and the supply of labour?
back: There is a **positive relationship**: the higher the wage rate, the **greater the supply of labour** in that occupation.

front: How do skills and qualifications affect the supply of labour?
back: A greater number of relevant graduates **increases the supply of labour** to specific industries. For example, more medical graduates raise the supply of nurses and doctors.

front: How does a larger population affect the supply of labour?
back: A larger population means **more people are available for work**, increasing the supply of labour.

front: How can net migration affect the supply of labour?
back: Policies that **increase the net migration rate** increase the supply of labour to certain industries.

front: What is meant by the participation rate?
back: The **participation rate** is the number of people **willing to work** within the working age group.

front:
**True or False?**

A youthful population tends to reduce the supply of labour.
back:
**False.**

A more youthful population, common in less developed countries, **increases the supply of labour**; an ageing population reduces it.

front:
**True or False?**

Raising the school leaving age tends to decrease the supply of labour.
back:
**True.**

A rise in the school leaving age keeps young people out of work, **reducing the supply of labour**.

front:
**True or False?**

A shrinking population would lead to a decrease in the supply of labour.
back:
**True.**

A fall in population reduces the number of people available to work, **decreasing the supply of labour**.

front: India's growing population has led to a rightward <u>  </u> in the supply of labour.
back: India's growing population has led to a rightward **shift** in the supply of labour.

front: If a worker's skill base is <u>  </u> between occupations, their occupational mobility is high.
back: If a worker's skill base is **transferable** between occupations, their occupational mobility is high.

front: Define **labour market equilibrium**.
back: **Labour market equilibrium** occurs when the **demand for labour** equals the **supply of labour**.

front: Define a **price taker** in the labour market.
back: A **price taker** is a firm that must **accept the wage rate** being paid to workers in the industry.

front: In the labour market, who demands labour and who supplies it?
back: **Firms demand** labour in order to produce output, while **workers (households) supply** their labour.

front: What happens if a firm offers a wage below the market rate?
back: If a firm offers a lower wage, it will likely **struggle to recruit workers**.

front: What happens if a firm offers a wage above the market rate?
back: If a firm offers a higher wage, there will be an **excess supply of workers** applying to work there.

front: How does a rise in the demand for labour affect the equilibrium wage and quantity?
back: A rise in the demand for labour **increases both the equilibrium wage rate and the quantity of labour employed**.

front: How does a fall in the supply of labour affect the equilibrium wage and quantity?
back: A fall in the supply of labour **raises the equilibrium wage rate** but **reduces the quantity of labour employed**.

front: Which way does the demand curve shift when demand for labour rises?
back: When demand for labour rises, the demand curve **shifts to the right**.

front:
**True or False?**

A fall in the supply of labour to an industry can be caused by workers switching to other occupations.
back:
**True.**

When workers move to different occupations, the supply of labour to the original industry falls. For example, graphic designers switching jobs reduces supply in that industry.

front:
**True or False?**

An individual firm in a competitive labour market can set its own wage rate.
back:
**False.**

An individual firm is a **price taker** and must accept the wage rate paid across the industry.

front: A rise in the demand for websites causes a rise in the demand for graphic designers, an example of <u>  </u> demand.
back: A rise in the demand for websites causes a rise in the demand for graphic designers, an example of **derived** demand.

front: A fall in the supply of labour shifts the labour supply curve to the <u>  </u>.
back: A fall in the supply of labour shifts the labour supply curve to the **left**.

front: Define **trade union**.
back: A **trade union** is an organisation that **represents the interests of its workers** in negotiations with a firm's management or owners.

front: Define **collective bargaining**.
back: **Collective bargaining** is when a trade union negotiates with employers **on behalf of all its members**, for example over wages and conditions.

front: Define **industrial action**.
back: **Industrial action** refers to methods such as strikes and overtime bans used to **force employers or governments to keep engaging** with a union.

front: Besides pay, name two interests that a trade union represents on behalf of workers.
back: Trade unions also represent workers' **health and safety** at work and the **reduction of discrimination and exploitation**.

front: What is a subscription in the context of trade unions?
back: A **subscription** is the **monthly fee** workers pay to join a trade union; membership ends when they stop paying it.

front: Which type of union represents workers in the same industry regardless of skill or seniority?
back: An **industrial union** represents **workers in the same industry**, whatever their skill level or seniority.

front: Which type of union represents professional office-based workers?
back: A **white collar union** represents professional **office-based workers**, such as financial advisors and teachers.

front: How can collective bargaining affect wages?
back: Through collective bargaining, workers have the **power to increase wages** above the level they could negotiate individually.

front: Name two examples of industrial action a trade union can take.
back: Examples of industrial action include **strikes** and **overtime bans** (also work to rule and go-slows).

front:
**True or False?**

A general union can be joined by skilled and unskilled workers in any industry.
back:
**True.**

A **general union** represents **skilled and unskilled workers in any industry**, such as truck drivers and musicians.

front:
**True or False?**

Trade union intervention leaves equilibrium wages and employment unchanged.
back:
**False.**

Trade union intervention **changes the equilibrium wages and employment** in the labour market.

front: As well as collective bargaining, trade union members benefit from legal <u>  </u> in disputes.
back: As well as collective bargaining, trade union members benefit from legal **representation** in disputes.

front: Trade unions negotiate with government on the creation and maintenance of <u>  </u> levels.
back: Trade unions negotiate with government on the creation and maintenance of **minimum wage** levels.

front: Define **indirect tax**.
back: An **indirect tax** is a tax levied by the government on **producers**, increasing their **cost of production**, which is passed on to consumers as a higher price.

front: Define **subsidy**.
back: A **subsidy** is a payment to a firm that **reduces the costs of production** and encourages an increase in the **output** of a good or service.

front: Define **internalising the externality**.
back: **Internalising the externality** means forcing producers to pay for the **external costs** of their activity, for example by taxing air pollution to raise the cost of production.

front: Which intervention suits an over-provided good?
back: An over-provided good is best addressed with an **indirect tax**, which raises its price and reduces consumption or production.

front: Which intervention suits an under-consumed good?
back: An under-provided or under-consumed good is best addressed with a **subsidy**, which lowers its price and increases output and consumption.

front: Why can a sugar tax fail to cut consumption much?
back: A sugar tax may fail to cut consumption much because demand can be **price inelastic**, so consumers keep buying despite the higher price.

front: Give one advantage of indirect taxes for the government.
back: Indirect taxes **raise revenue** for the government, which could be used to fund healthcare and education initiatives.

front: Give one disadvantage of subsidies for producers.
back: Subsidies can **discourage firms from becoming more efficient or competitive**, as they become reliant on financial assistance from governments.

front:
**True or False?**

A subsidy raises the price of a good.
back:
**False.**

A subsidy lowers the cost of production and therefore reduces the price of a good.

front:
**True or False?**

Indirect taxes can create illegal markets as consumers try to avoid paying them.
back:
**True.**

Consumers may seek to avoid the tax, creating illegal markets for the taxed good.

front:
**True or False?**

Sin taxes tend to fall hardest on high-income consumers.
back:
**False.**

Sin taxes often affect low-income consumers disproportionately, worsening inequality.

front: Subsidies may disproportionately benefit <u>  </u> consumers, for example subsidies on electric vehicles.
back: Subsidies may disproportionately benefit **higher-income** consumers, for example subsidies on electric vehicles.

front: There is an <u>  </u> associated with government spending on subsidies.
back: There is an **opportunity cost** associated with government spending on subsidies.

front: Define **regulation**.
back: **Regulation** is the process of monitoring and enforcing laws aimed at limiting the harm caused by the **external costs** of consumption or production.

front: Define **fine**.
back: A **fine** is a monetary penalty imposed for breaking laws or regulations.

front: Define **pollution permit**.
back: A **pollution permit** allows a firm to pollute up to a certain amount, and any surplus can be sold to other firms for additional revenue.

front: What determines the price of a pollution permit?
back: The price of a pollution permit is determined by **demand and supply** in the permit market.

front: Why are regulatory agencies created?
back: Regulatory agencies are created to **enforce the law** and ensure that regulations are not broken.

front: When will a firm switch to cleaner technology under a permit scheme?
back: A firm will switch to cleaner technology when the **price of additional permits is greater than the cost of investing** in new pollution technology.

front: Give one advantage of using fines and regulation.
back: Fines and regulation act as a **strong deterrent**, encouraging individuals and businesses to comply with the law.

front: Give one disadvantage of pollution permits.
back: A disadvantage is that firms may **relocate production** to places where they can pollute without limits.

front:
**True or False?**

A fine can generate extra revenue for the government.
back:
**True.**

Fines can generate extra government revenue as well as deterring harmful behaviour.

front:
**True or False?**

Issuing too many pollution permits strengthens the incentive to cut pollution.
back:
**False.**

If the government issues too many permits, allowing high pollution levels, there is little incentive to reduce pollution.

front:
**True or False?**

Regulation can create underground illegal markets.
back:
**True.**

Regulation may create underground illegal markets, which could generate even higher external costs on society.

front: The cost of a permit becomes an additional cost of production, which should reduce <u>  </u>.
back: The cost of a permit becomes an additional cost of production, which should reduce **supply**.

front: Heavy-polluting firms have to <u>  </u> additional permits from less-polluting firms.
back: Heavy-polluting firms have to **buy** additional permits from less-polluting firms.

front: Define **competition policy**.
back: **Competition policy** is government policy that aims to make **markets more competitive** and to ensure that the **public interest is protected**.

front: Define **deregulation**.
back: **Deregulation** is the removal of government regulations that raise industry costs or act as a **barrier to entry**, promoting competition and contestability.

front: Define **privatisation**.
back: **Privatisation** is the sale of a government-owned firm to the private sector, which encourages new entrants who feel they can compete more effectively.

front: Name the three main forms of consumer exploitation.
back: The main forms of consumer exploitation are **higher prices**, **lack of choice** and **poor quality products**.

front: How does competitive tendering promote competition?
back: Competitive tendering lets the private sector bid to supply government contracts, which generates **more private sector activity** and increases competition.

front: What does price regulation do to a monopoly?
back: Price regulation sets **maximum prices** on a monopoly in order to lower prices and increase output.

front: How can a regulator allow a merger while protecting competition?
back: A regulator can allow a merger but insist the new firm **sells certain assets**, which limits its market share.

front: Which UK law gives consumers rights to refunds and repairs?
back: The **Consumer Rights Act 2015** gives consumers rights to refunds, repairs or replacements if goods are faulty, not as described or not fit for purpose.

front: Give one drawback of competition policy.
back: Competition policy can reduce monopoly profits used for R&D, leading to **less innovative products** and production processes.

front:
**True or False?**

Monopolists can restrict output and raise prices.
back:
**True.**

Monopolists can restrict output and raise prices, which is not in the best interest of consumers.

front:
**True or False?**

Profit regulation gives monopolies a strong incentive to lower their costs.
back:
**False.**

Profit regulation gives no incentive to lower costs, so if costs are high, consumers end up paying higher prices.

front:
**True or False?**

Competition policy can be expensive and time consuming to enforce.
back:
**True.**

It can be expensive and time consuming to ensure firms or industries are complying with competition policies.

front: A key function of a regulator is to monitor merger and <u>  </u> activity.
back: A key function of a regulator is to monitor merger and **takeover** activity.

front: Providing tax incentives or subsidies to <u>  </u> can increase the number of new entrants.
back: Providing tax incentives or subsidies to **small firms** can increase the number of new entrants.

front: Define **minimum wage**.
back: A **minimum wage** is a legally imposed wage level that employers must pay their workers, set **above** the market rate.

front: Define **excess supply of labour**.
back: **Excess supply of labour** occurs when the quantity of labour supplied exceeds the quantity demanded, creating the potential for **unemployment**.

front: What is the main aim of a minimum wage?
back: The main aim of a minimum wage is to **improve equity** and avoid the **exploitation** of workers.

front: Which sectors are most affected by a minimum wage?
back: A minimum wage most affects workers in lower-paid sectors such as **retail, hospitality and agriculture**.

front: What happens to labour supply when a minimum wage is imposed?
back: When a minimum wage is imposed above the market rate, the **supply of labour increases** as workers are incentivised by the higher wage.

front: What happens to labour demand when a minimum wage is imposed?
back: When a minimum wage is imposed, the **demand for labour by firms decreases** because they face higher production costs.

front: Give one advantage of a minimum wage.
back: A minimum wage guarantees a **minimum income** for the lowest paid workers, helping to improve their standard of living.

front: How can a minimum wage lead to lower government tax revenues?
back: If a minimum wage raises firms' costs and increases **unemployment**, government tax revenues fall and benefit payments rise.

front:
**True or False?**

A minimum wage can raise firms' costs of production, which they may pass on as higher prices.
back:
**True.**

Higher wage costs may lead firms to raise the prices of their goods and services.

front:
**True or False?**

Raising the minimum wage further increases the excess supply of labour.
back:
**True.**

Raising the minimum wage further distorts the market, contracting labour demand and extending labour supply, increasing the excess supply of labour.

front:
**True or False?**

A minimum wage always increases unemployment.
back:
**False.**

Higher wages can raise consumption and total demand, increasing firms' demand for labour, so unemployment does not always rise.

front: The level of the minimum wage often varies based on a worker's <u>  </u>.
back: The level of the minimum wage often varies based on a worker's **age**.

front: A minimum wage may incentivise workers to be more <u>  </u>, helping to offset higher wages.
back: A minimum wage may incentivise workers to be more **productive**, helping to offset higher wages.

front: Define **macroeconomic objectives**.
back: **Macroeconomic objectives** are goals set by the government aimed at improving a country's overall **economic performance** and the **quality of life** of its citizens.

front: Define **economic growth**.
back: **Economic growth** is the **annual increase** in the level of national output, as measured by **gross domestic product (GDP)**.

front: Define **gross domestic product (GDP)**.
back: **Gross domestic product (GDP)** is the **total value** of all goods and services produced in an economy in a year.

front: Define **GDP per capita**.
back: **GDP per capita** is GDP divided by the population, showing the **mean wealth** of each citizen in a country.

front: Give one benefit of strong economic growth.
back: Strong economic growth brings **higher incomes**, **lower unemployment** and better government budgets.

front: What annual growth rate do many developed nations target?
back: Many developed nations target an annual growth rate of **2–3%**, considered to be **sustainable growth**.

front: Why can high economic growth and stable prices conflict?
back: High economic growth and stable prices can conflict because **growth can drive up the general price level**, causing inflation.

front: Why is GDP per capita a better measure for comparing living standards?
back: GDP per capita is better because it shows the **mean wealth per citizen**, making it easier to compare **standards of living** between countries.

front:
**True or False?**

GDP per capita reveals how income is distributed within a country.
back:
**False.**

GDP per capita is an **average**, so it hides significant **differences** in the standard of living within the same country.

front:
**True or False?**

GDP includes the value of unpaid and voluntary work.
back:
**False.**

GDP does **not** include unpaid or voluntary work, so it understates activity such as family childcare provision.

front: Sustainable economic growth is less likely to cause excessive <u>  </u> inflation.
back: Sustainable economic growth is less likely to cause excessive **demand-pull** inflation.

front: A stable current account balance of payments primarily considers the value of trade in a nation's <u>  </u>.
back: A stable current account balance of payments primarily considers the value of trade in a nation's **exports and imports**.

front: Define the **economic (business) cycle**.
back: The **economic (business) cycle** describes the **upturns and downturns** in the level of a country's economic activity (GDP) over time.

front: Define **recession**.
back: A **recession** occurs when an economy experiences **two consecutive quarters (6 months) or more of negative GDP growth**.

front: Define **slump**.
back: A **slump** is an **extended period of negative GDP growth**, usually with high unemployment and business failure.

front: Define **boom**.
back: A **boom** is a period when an economy experiences an extended period of **increasing rates of GDP growth**, with high incomes, high inflation and low unemployment.

front: What happens to business and consumer confidence during a recession?
back: During a recession, business and consumer **confidence tend to be low**, and business profits fall.

front: What happens to unemployment during the growth stage?
back: During the growth stage, rising production levels lead to a **rise in employment levels**, so unemployment falls.

front: How does economic growth affect standards of living?
back: Economic growth raises employment and incomes, and higher tax revenue can fund **health and education** and **redistribute income**, improving standards of living.

front: How is growth in productive potential shown on a PPC?
back: Growth in productive potential is shown by an **outward shift of the entire PPC**.

front:
**True or False?**

During a recession, deflation may set in as demand falls.
back:
**True.**

As incomes and consumer demand fall during a recession, deflation may set in.

front:
**True or False?**

Economic growth can harm the environment through negative externalities.
back:
**True.**

Rising growth increases negative externalities of production and consumption, depleting resources more rapidly.

front: During the growth stage, rising disposable incomes lead to increased <u>  </u> for products.
back: During the growth stage, rising disposable incomes lead to increased **demand** for products.

front: An outward shift of the PPC is caused by an increase in the quality or quantity of the available <u>  </u>.
back: An outward shift of the PPC is caused by an increase in the quality or quantity of the available **factors of production**.

front: Define **inflation**.
back: **Inflation** is the **sustained increase** in the **average price level** of goods and services in an economy.

front: Define **deflation**.
back: **Deflation** occurs when there is a **fall in the average price level** of goods and services, meaning the percentage change in prices falls below zero.

front: Define **disinflation**.
back: **Disinflation** occurs when the average price level is still **rising**, but **at a lower rate** than before.

front: Define the **consumer price index (CPI)**.
back: The **consumer price index (CPI)** is a measure of inflation based on the changing price of a 'household basket' of over 700 goods and services.

front: How do the contents of the CPI basket change over time?
back: Each year some goods and services **exit the basket** and **new ones are added** to reflect changing spending habits.

front: Why is a low and stable rate of inflation important for firms?
back: A low and stable rate of inflation lets firms **confidently plan for future investment** and offers **price stability** to consumers.

front: Why are goods in the CPI basket weighted?
back: Goods are **weighted** according to the **proportion of household spending** on them, so items bought more often, like food, carry a greater weight.

front: What is the inflation rate if the CPI rises from 100 to 107?
back: If the CPI rises from 100 to 107, the inflation rate is **7%**.

front:
**True or False?**

A fall in the inflation rate from 5% to 3% means prices are falling.
back:
**False.**

Prices are still **rising**, just more slowly; a falling inflation rate is called **disinflation**.

front:
**True or False?**

The CPI is calculated using an index with 100 as the base year.
back:
**True.**

The inflation rate is calculated using an index with **100 as the base year**.

front: Each month, prices in the CPI basket are collected from hundreds of <u>  </u> across the country.
back: Each month, prices in the CPI basket are collected from hundreds of **locations** across the country.

front: The CPI basket is compiled using a household <u>  </u> survey to determine its contents.
back: The CPI basket is compiled using a household **expenditure** survey to determine its contents.

front: Define **demand-pull inflation**.
back: **Demand-pull inflation** is caused by **excess demand** in the economy, which pushes prices up as suppliers raise them to balance the demand-supply gap.

front: Define **cost-push inflation**.
back: **Cost-push inflation** is caused by **increases in the costs of production**, which firms pass on to consumers as **higher prices**.

front: Define **menu costs**.
back: **Menu costs** are the costs firms face from having to update their menus or price cards when inflation forces price changes.

front: Define **shoe leather costs**.
back: **Shoe leather costs** are the hidden costs or waste of resources during high inflation, such as people spending more time searching for a better deal.

front: How can inflation reduce a worker's purchasing power?
back: If prices rise faster than incomes, **real purchasing power falls**, so workers can afford less with the same income.

front: What causes cost-push inflation?
back: Cost-push inflation is caused by **rising costs of production**, such as increases in raw materials, labour or interest rates.

front: How does a rise in oil prices cause inflation?
back: A rise in oil prices increases the **cost of production** for goods relying on oil, causing **cost-push inflation**.

front: How does inflation affect a country's exports?
back: Inflation **erodes the international competitiveness** of exports, as they become relatively more expensive, which may slow economic growth.

front: How can lowering the central bank base rate cause inflation?
back: A lower base rate increases **borrowing**, raising consumption and investment, which can lead to **demand-pull inflation**.

front:
**True or False?**

Cost-push inflation is caused by excess demand in the economy.
back:
**False.**

Excess demand causes **demand-pull** inflation; cost-push inflation is caused by rising costs of production.

front:
**True or False?**

There is generally an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment.
back:
**True.**

Generally, when inflation increases unemployment decreases, and vice versa.

front: The aim is to have a low and stable rate of inflation of approximately <u>  </u>.
back: The aim is to have a low and stable rate of inflation of approximately **2%**.

front: Lower taxes raise disposable income, which can create excess demand and <u>  </u> inflation.
back: Lower taxes raise disposable income, which can create excess demand and **demand-pull** inflation.

front: Define **unemployment**.
back: **Unemployment** occurs when a person is not working but is actively seeking work.

front: Define **employment**.
back: **Employment** refers to the economic use of labour as a factor of production.

front: Define the **labour force**.
back: The **labour force** consists of all workers actively working plus the unemployed who are seeking work.

front: Define **structural unemployment**.
back: **Structural unemployment** occurs when there is a mismatch between jobs and skills in the economy.

front: Define **frictional unemployment**.
back: **Frictional unemployment** occurs when workers are between jobs, and is usually short-term.

front: Which survey is used to measure unemployment in many countries?
back: Unemployment is measured in many countries using the **International Labour Organisation (ILO) Survey**.

front: What causes cyclical unemployment?
back: Cyclical unemployment is caused by a **fall in total (aggregate) demand** in the economy.

front: What is the formula for the unemployment rate?
back: The unemployment rate = **(number actively seeking ÷ total labour force) × 100**.

front: A country has a labour force of 2,400,000 and 1,800,000 people employed. What is its unemployment rate?
back: With 600,000 unemployed, the unemployment rate is **25%** (600,000 ÷ 2,400,000 × 100).

front:
**True or False?**

Seasonal unemployment occurs when labour is not required until the next season.
back:
**True.**

Seasonal unemployment happens as certain seasons end, for example fruit pickers or ski instructors.

front:
**True or False?**

Pensioners and school children are part of the labour force.
back:
**False.**

Pensioners and school children are in the non-labour force, as they are economically inactive.

front: The ILO survey is sent to a random sample of households every <u>  </u>.
back: The ILO survey is sent to a random sample of households every **quarter**.

front: Voluntary unemployment occurs when workers <u>  </u> to be unemployed.
back: Voluntary unemployment occurs when workers **choose** to be unemployed, for example while waiting to find a job with higher wages.

front: Define **consumer and business confidence**.
back: **Consumer and business confidence** is the level of optimism that consumers and businesses have regarding their expected financial situation.

front: How does high unemployment affect national output?
back: High unemployment reduces consumer incomes, so **demand for goods and services falls** and firms reduce output.

front: How does high unemployment affect government finances?
back: Governments receive **less tax revenue** and have **higher expenditures** on welfare payments.

front: How does high unemployment affect poverty?
back: **Poverty rises** as incomes fall, so some workers struggle to afford basic necessities such as food, shelter and clothing.

front: What happened to Greece's unemployment during the 2009–2013 recession?
back: Greece's unemployment reached **27%**, with youth unemployment peaking at **60%**.

front: Why do consumers save more when unemployment is high?
back: Consumers save more because they have **less job security**.

front: How does high unemployment affect business investment?
back: Businesses expect to receive less sales revenue, so they **delay their investment plans**.

front: How does unemployment affect the use of scarce resources?
back: As the economy contracts, there is a more **inefficient use of available resources**.

front:
**True or False?**

High unemployment tends to increase inequality in society.
back:
**True.**

Inequalities rise as some individuals struggle to access healthcare and education, and crime rates may increase.

front:
**True or False?**

High unemployment can lead to an increase in crime rates.
back:
**True.**

Unemployment can cause wider societal problems, such as an increase in crime rates.

front: During a recession, high poverty rates can also lead to rising levels of <u>  </u>.
back: During a recession, high poverty rates can also lead to rising levels of **homelessness**.

front: As inequality rises, some individuals struggle to access healthcare and <u>  </u>.
back: As inequality rises, some individuals struggle to access healthcare and **education**.

front: Define the **Balance of Payments (BoP)**.
back: The **Balance of Payments** is a record of all the financial transactions that occur between a country and the rest of the world.

front: Define a **current account deficit**.
back: A **current account deficit** occurs when the value of outflows is greater than the value of inflows, usually when imports exceed exports.

front: Define a **current account surplus**.
back: A **current account surplus** occurs when the value of inflows is greater than the value of outflows, usually when exports exceed imports.

front: What does the current account mainly record?
back: The current account mainly records the financial transactions related to **exports and imports of goods and services**.

front: What are visible exports and imports?
back: Visible exports and imports are trade in **goods**.

front: Do imports represent a leakage or an injection?
back: Imports represent a **leakage** of money from the economy.

front: How can a country running a deficit move its current account towards positive?
back: **Export-led economic growth** would help a deficit country's current account become positive.

front: How can the quality of domestic goods cause a current account deficit?
back: If a country develops a reputation for **poor quality**, its exports fall and imports rise, causing a deficit.

front: Why did Germany run a trade surplus in 2023?
back: Germany's **€209.4 billion** surplus reflected strong exports of cars, machinery and engineering.

front:
**True or False?**

A depreciation of a country's currency tends to improve its current account balance.
back:
**True.**

A weaker currency makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, so exports rise and imports fall, improving the current account.

front:
**True or False?**

Rising income and wealth in an economy tends to push the current account towards a surplus.
back:
**False.**

Rising income and wealth increase the value of imports, which pushes the balance towards a deficit.

front: Services are also referred to as <u>  </u> exports and imports.
back: Services are also referred to as **invisible** exports and imports.

front: In 2023, China had a trade <u>  </u> of \$823.2 billion, driven by competitively priced electronics.
back: In 2023, China had a trade **surplus** of \$823.2 billion, driven by competitively priced electronics.

front: Define the **exchange rate**.
back: The **exchange rate** is the relative price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency.

front: Define currency **appreciation**.
back: A currency **appreciation** occurs when the value of a currency rises, making exports relatively more expensive and imports less expensive.

front: Define currency **depreciation**.
back: A currency **depreciation** occurs when the value of a currency falls, making exports relatively more attractive and imports less attractive.

front: How does an appreciation affect the current account balance?
back: An appreciation often leads to a **worsening** of the current account balance.

front: How does a depreciation affect a nation's exports?
back: A depreciation makes exports relatively cheaper, so **exports rise** and the current account improves.

front: How can a current account deficit affect unemployment?
back: With falling demand for locally produced goods, fewer workers are required, so **unemployment rises**.

front: Why might a current account deficit slow economic growth?
back: Exports are a key component of real GDP, so a fall in exports can **significantly reduce economic growth**.

front: What does the J-curve effect describe?
back: The J-curve shows there is a **time lag** before a currency depreciation improves the current account balance.

front:
**True or False?**

A currency appreciation makes a nation's imports cheaper.
back:
**True.**

An appreciation raises the currency's value, making imports less expensive and exports dearer.

front:
**True or False?**

Following a depreciation, the current account improves immediately.
back:
**False.**

The J-curve shows the current account initially worsens before it improves.

front: A currency depreciation makes a nation's imports more <u>  </u>.
back: A currency depreciation makes a nation's imports more **expensive**.

front: A current account deficit driven by rising imports is often financed through higher levels of <u>  </u>.
back: A current account deficit driven by rising imports is often financed through higher levels of **borrowing**.

front: In the short run, the combined price elasticity of demand for exports and imports is <u>  </u>, so the trade balance worsens.
back: In the short run, the combined price elasticity of demand for exports and imports is **inelastic** (less than one), so the trade balance worsens.

front: Define **external cost**.
back: An **external cost** is a cost of production that falls on third parties or the environment, rather than on the business itself.

front: Define **visual pollution**.
back: **Visual pollution** is business activity that makes a landscape look like an **eyesore**, such as litter, mine dumps or chimney smoke.

front: Define **noise pollution**.
back: **Noise pollution** is excessive noise that causes stress or hearing loss, from sources such as loud machinery, factories, traffic, bars or restaurants.

front: Define **water pollution**.
back: **Water pollution** is the contamination of rivers, lakes and oceans with harmful substances such as pesticides, fertilisers or chemicals.

front: Which gases are released when fossil fuels are burned, causing air pollution?
back: Burning fossil fuels releases **greenhouse gases** into the atmosphere, increasing air pollution.

front: Which airport is used as an example of noise pollution from air traffic?
back: **Heathrow airport** is used as an example, where noise from arriving and departing flights impacts local residents.

front: Which business activity in Ecuador has been linked to water pollution?
back: **Pesticide use in banana farming** in Ecuador has been linked to water pollution, posing risks to river quality.

front: What health illnesses has air pollution in China been linked to?
back: Air pollution in China has been linked to **respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses**.

front:
**True or False?**

Governments are increasingly setting macroeconomic targets based around environmental protection.
back:
**True.**

Governments are doing more and more to set **macroeconomic targets** based around environmental protection.

front:
**True or False?**

Before its plastic bag ban, Kenya suffered visual pollution from plastic bags littering streets and rivers.
back:
**True.**

Plastic bags littering streets, rivers and natural environments are an example of visual pollution.

front: Business activity can create external <u>  </u> when providing a good or service.
back: Business activity can create external **costs of production** when providing a good or service.

front: Types of pollution that create external costs to the environment include visual, air, noise and <u>  </u> pollution.
back: Types of pollution that create external costs to the environment include visual, air, noise and **water** pollution.

front: Define **plastic tax**.
back: A **plastic tax** is a charge firms must pay whenever they import plastic packaging into the country, aimed at reducing plastic use.

front: Define **pollution permit**.
back: A **pollution permit** is a licence allowing a firm to emit a set amount of pollution, which can be bought or sold to create an incentive to cut emissions.

front: Define **public good**.
back: A **public good**, such as a park, is a free open space that people can use without paying, so it is not a source of income for the government.

front: Roughly how many plastic bags are produced worldwide each year?
back: Over **5 trillion** plastic bags are produced around the world each year.

front: How many people are impacted by flight noise at Heathrow airport?
back: Over **700,000** people are impacted by the noise from flights at Heathrow airport.

front: How much carbon dioxide did coal powered plants emit in 2022?
back: Coal powered plants emitted **15.22 billion metric tonnes** of carbon dioxide in 2022.

front: Which government intervention is used to tackle agricultural water pollution?
back: Governments use **regulation and fines** on surface and ground water quality to reduce contamination from fertilisers and pesticides.

front: How many national parks does the Canadian government provide?
back: The Canadian government provides **48 national parks** to conserve land, protect ecosystems and provide recreational activities.

front: Name one regulation Heathrow uses to reduce aircraft noise.
back: Heathrow uses a **limit on flights between 11:30pm and 6:00am**, alongside variable landing charges linked to noise and noise insulation around the perimeter.

front:
**True or False?**

Governments usually rely on a single policy to protect the environment.
back:
**False.**

Governments use a **combination** of policies, such as regulation, fines, taxation and subsidies, to protect the environment.

front:
**True or False?**

Using land for parks involves an opportunity cost.
back:
**True.**

The land could be used for alternative purposes such as housing, schools or hospitals, so providing parks has an **opportunity cost**.

front: Plastic can take <u>  </u> years to break down.
back: Plastic can take **500-1000** years to break down.

front: Higher variable landing charges give airlines an incentive to invest in <u>  </u> planes.
back: Higher variable landing charges give airlines an incentive to invest in **noise-reducing** planes.

front: Define **equality**.
back: **Equality** describes situations where economic outcomes are similar for different people or different social groups.

front: Define **absolute poverty**.
back: **Absolute poverty** is a situation where individuals cannot afford the **basic necessities** for a healthy and safe existence, such as shelter, water, nutrition, clothing and healthcare.

front: Define **relative poverty**.
back: **Relative poverty** is a situation where household income is a certain percentage less than the **median household income** in the economy.

front: How did the World Bank define absolute poverty in 2022?
back: In 2022, the **World Bank** defined absolute poverty as living on less than **\$2.15 a day**, the international poverty line.

front: Below what share of median household income is a household in relative poverty?
back: Households living with less than **50% of the median household income** are considered to be in relative poverty.

front: In which type of country is absolute poverty more prevalent?
back: Absolute poverty is more prevalent in **developing countries** than in developed ones.

front: Under capitalism, why do higher-skilled workers earn more?
back: Under capitalism, **inequality is inevitable** because workers with higher skills receive higher wages while low-skilled workers receive little to no wage.

front: Name one reason to reduce poverty and inequality.
back: Reasons include **meeting basic needs**, improving standards of living and addressing ethical considerations.

front:
**True or False?**

Relative poverty is the main form of poverty that occurs in developed countries.
back:
**True.**

Relative poverty is the main form of poverty in **developed** countries, while absolute poverty is more common in developing ones.

front:
**True or False?**

A progressive tax system charges lower income earners a lower tax rate than higher income earners.
back:
**True.**

Under a **progressive** tax system, lower income earners pay a lower tax rate than higher income earners.

front: According to the United Nations, an estimated <u>  </u> people will experience hunger and malnutrition by 2030.
back: According to the United Nations, an estimated **600 million** people will experience hunger and malnutrition by 2030.

front: Inequality in the distribution of income is one cause of absolute and relative <u>  </u>.
back: Inequality in the distribution of income is one cause of absolute and relative **poverty**.

front: Define **progressive tax**.
back: A **progressive tax** is one where, as income rises, a larger percentage of income is paid in tax, redistributing income from higher to lower earners.

front: Define **regressive tax**.
back: A **regressive tax** is one where, as income rises, a smaller percentage of income is paid in tax; all indirect taxes are regressive.

front: Define **benefit payments**.
back: **Benefit payments** are transfers usually given to the poorest and most vulnerable, such as unemployment, disability, pension and child benefits.

front: Name the three main methods governments use to redistribute income.
back: The three main methods are **progressive taxation, benefit payments and investment in education and healthcare**.

front: Do most countries rely only on progressive taxes?
back: No. Most countries use a **mix of progressive (direct) and regressive (indirect) taxes**.

front: What type of policy is investment in education and healthcare?
back: Investment in education and healthcare is a **supply-side policy** that increases the potential output of the country.

front: Which country is used as an example of high social welfare and benefit payments?
back: **Denmark** is used as an example, transferring income to low income households through unemployment benefits and housing assistance.

front: How does investment in healthcare help redistribute income?
back: Healthcare investment leads to a **healthier, more productive workforce**, raising output and incomes.

front:
**True or False?**

A progressive tax system can deter investment.
back:
**True.**

Progressive taxes on capital gains and dividends can deter investment, which may slow economic growth.

front:
**True or False?**

The aim of redistribution is a completely equal distribution of income.
back:
**False.**

The aim is a more **fair or equitable** distribution of income, not a completely equal one.

front:
**True or False?**

High levels of benefit payments can act as a disincentive to work.
back:
**True.**

High benefit payments can act as a **disincentive to work**, with some households becoming dependent on them.

front: Investment in education and healthcare shifts the production possibility frontier <u>  </u>.
back: Investment in education and healthcare shifts the production possibility frontier **outwards**.

front: A <u>  </u> of policies is the most effective way to tackle poverty and inequality.
back: A **blend** of policies is the most effective way to tackle poverty and inequality.

front: Define **fiscal policy**.
back: **Fiscal policy** is the use of **government spending and taxation** to influence economic growth and achieve macroeconomic objectives.

front: Define **direct tax**.
back: A **direct tax** is a tax imposed on **income and profits** and paid directly to the government by the individual or firm.

front: Define **indirect tax**.
back: An **indirect tax** is a tax imposed on **goods and services**, which the supplier is responsible for paying to the government.

front: Define **transfer payment**.
back: A **transfer payment** is a government payment for which **no goods or services are exchanged**, such as unemployment benefits.

front: Who is responsible for setting fiscal policy?
back: The **government** is responsible for setting fiscal policy.

front: What is the main source of government revenue?
back: The main source of government revenue is **taxation**.

front: Give one reason why governments levy taxes.
back: Governments levy taxes to **fund government expenditure**, as well as to discourage demerit goods and redistribute income.

front: What does current expenditure refer to?
back: Current expenditure refers to the **day-to-day spending** required to run the government and public sector, such as public-sector wages.

front:
**True or False?**

Capital expenditure is government spending on infrastructure, such as new hospitals and railways.
back:
**True.**

Capital expenditure is spending on infrastructure and capital equipment, such as new hospitals, schools and high-speed rail. This differs from current expenditure, which covers day-to-day running costs.

front:
**True or False?**

Fiscal policy is used to help the government achieve its macroeconomic objectives.
back:
**True.**

Fiscal policy aims to stabilise economic growth, control inflation and maintain low unemployment.

front: A tax imposed on imported goods, used to reduce the volume of imports, is known as a <u>  </u>.
back: A tax imposed on imported goods, used to reduce the volume of imports, is known as a **tariff**.

front: The government presents its fiscal policy each year when it delivers the annual <u>  </u>.
back: The government presents its fiscal policy each year when it delivers the annual **Budget**.

front: Define **fiscal deficit**.
back: A **fiscal deficit** occurs when **government revenue is less than government expenditure**.

front: Define **fiscal surplus**.
back: A **fiscal surplus** occurs when **government revenue is greater than government expenditure**.

front: Define **balanced budget**.
back: A **balanced budget** occurs when **government revenue equals government expenditure**.

front: Define **crowding out**.
back: **Crowding out** occurs when government borrowing drives up interest rates, reducing private-sector borrowing and investment.

front: How is a fiscal deficit financed?
back: A fiscal deficit is financed through **public sector borrowing**.

front: What happens to national debt when a government runs a fiscal deficit?
back: National debt **rises**, as the government spends more than it receives and must repay the borrowing with interest.

front: Give one use of a fiscal surplus.
back: A fiscal surplus can be used to **fund capital expenditure on infrastructure**, or to pay back government debt.

front: Why might a fiscal surplus slow economic growth?
back: A surplus can slow growth because the government **withdraws more through higher taxes than it injects through spending** into the circular flow of income.

front:
**True or False?**

A government may deliberately run a fiscal surplus to slow growth and reduce inflationary pressure.
back:
**True.**

By withdrawing more through taxes than it injects through spending, a surplus can moderate economic growth and ease pressure on prices.

front:
**True or False?**

A government can finance a fiscal deficit by borrowing from both domestic and foreign lenders.
back:
**True.**
